title: Exponentials and Radicals
lead: This class goes deeper into Advanced Math. The first half is the algebra of exponents: the rules, fraction exponents and radicals. The second half is exponential functions, the growth and decay models that fill Module 2 as word problems about populations, money and decay.

parts.title: Part 1 · The parts of an exponential expression
parts.html:
In 5x³, the 5 is the coefficient, x is the base and 3 is the exponent. The exponent applies only to what it is attached to: 5x³ means 5 · x · x · x.

Brackets change that. (5x)³ means 5x · 5x · 5x = 125x³. So 5x³ and (5x)³ are different expressions, and mixing them up is the most common slip in this topic.

An exponent can be any rational number: a whole number, a negative number or a fraction. A fraction exponent is another way of writing a root: x1/2 is the same as √x.

parts.title: Part 2 · The exponent rules
parts.html:
OperationRuleExample
Add or subtractOnly like terms: same base and same exponent. Combine the coefficients.4x3 + 2x3 = 6x3
Multiply, same baseMultiply the coefficients, add the exponents.2x3 · 5x4 = 10x7
Divide, same baseDivide the coefficients, subtract the exponents.12x5 / 4x2 = 3x3
Multiply or divide, same exponentMultiply or divide the bases, keep the exponent.23 · 53 = 103 = 1,000   and   122 / 42 = 32 = 9
Power of a powerRaise the coefficient to the power, multiply the exponents.(x4)2 = x8   and   (3x2)3 = 27x6
Negative exponentMove the base to the other side of the fraction bar and make the exponent positive.5x−2 = 5/x2
Zero exponentAny base except 0 raised to the power 0 is 1.x0 = 1, so 7x0 = 7

What cannot be combined. 3x² + 3x⁵ stays as it is: same base, different exponents. 2x² + 2y² stays as it is: same exponent, different bases.

Negative exponents in fractions. A negative exponent often appears after dividing, and a factor with a negative exponent switches between the top and the bottom of a fraction.

x3x8=x3−8=x−5=1x5x−2y−5=y5x2

Changing the base. When two numbers are powers of the same smaller number, rewrite them with that base. Then the same-base rules apply.

Write 2x·84 as a single power of 2.
8=23,  so  84=(23)4=2122x·212=2x+12

Look for this whenever a question mixes bases such as 2, 4 and 8, or 3, 9 and 27.

parts.title: Part 3 · Fraction exponents and radicals
parts.html:
A root undoes a power: √(5²) = 5. Writing the root as an exponent shows why. A square root is the power 1/2, so √(5²) = (5²)1/2 = 52 · 1/2 = 5¹.

Fraction exponents are roots: x1/2 = √x, x1/3 = ∛x, and in general the nth root of xm is xm/n. The power under the root sign goes on top of the fraction; the small number on the root sign goes on the bottom. A plain square root has a hidden 2 there.

x34=x34x5=x52823=(83)2=22=4

Every rule in Part 2 works the same way with fraction exponents: x1/2 · x1/3 = x1/2 + 1/3 = x5/6.

Multiplying and dividing roots. Roots of the same kind combine under one root sign:

xn·yn=xynxnyn=xyn

That gives you two routes, and you can pick whichever is shorter. With variables, converting to fraction exponents is usually easier. With numbers, combining under one root often gives a perfect square.

x5·x=x52·x12=x62=x32·50=100=10

Simplifying a root of a product. Take the root of each factor separately.

27x6y33=273·x63·y33=2713·x63·y33=3x2y

For “which expression is equivalent” questions, turn every root into a fraction exponent first, then apply the rules.

Solving radical equations: isolate the radical, square both sides, solve, then check.

x=x−2 Square: x=x2−4x+4 → x2−5x+4=0 → (x−4)(x−1)=0
Check x=4: 4=2 and 4−2=2 → works
Check x=1: 1=1 but 1−2=−1 → extraneous
Answer: x=4

Squaring can create fake solutions. Checking in the original equation is not optional.

A radical in a denominator. If an equation contains k/√x, then √x cannot be zero, so x > 0. Domain checks like this appear on hard questions: watch for choices that break the domain.

parts.title: Part 4 · Exponential functions
parts.html:
One mental move unlocks nearly all of these: read the base as a multiplier per time step.

An exponential function looks like f(t) = a · bt. The variable is in the exponent. Every time t increases by 1, the output is multiplied by b.

FunctionBehaviour
f(t) = 500 · 2tDoubles every step
f(t) = 100 · (0.5)tHalves every step (decay)
f(t) = 80 · (1.05)tGrows 5% per step

a is the starting value: at t = 0, b⁰ = 1, so f(0) = a. b is the multiplier per step.

Compare with linear. Linear adds the same amount each step (+3 each time). Exponential multiplies by the same amount each step (×1.05 each time). That contrast is itself a tested question: “which situation is modeled by an exponential function?”

parts.title: Part 5 · Reading percent change into the base
parts.html:
This is the skill the SAT tests most. Every percent change becomes a multiplier.

Change per periodBaseWhy
Increase of 5%1.05100% + 5% = 105% of the old amount
Decrease of 12%0.88You keep 88%
Doubling / halving / tripling2 / 0.5 / 3

Common mistake. “Decreases by 40%” is base 0.60, not 0.40: you keep 60%. And “increases by 700%” does not mean multiply by 7. The final amount is 800% of the original, a factor of 8. An increase of p% is always 1 + p/100.

Time steps that are not 1. If a quantity grows 2% per quarter and t is in years, there are 4 steps per year: a(1.02)4t. The exponent must count how many steps have passed. If the growth is p% every d days and t is in days, write a(1 + p/100)t/d. The check: at t = d the exponent is exactly 1, one full step.

Finding the rate from a model. In f(t) = 340(1.4)t/3, the exponent divides by 3, so the base applies once every 3 units of time: the quantity grows 40% every three days. Read a fraction in the exponent as “one step per d units”. For p(t) = 650 · 3t/240, the population triples every 240 days.

parts.title: Part 6 · Growth and decay word problems
parts.html:
1. Identify the starting value (a).
  2. Identify the percent change per step and convert it to a multiplier. Watch the increase-by-700% trap.
  3. Identify the step length and set the exponent so that one step makes it equal 1.
  4. Plug in what is asked.
A culture of 340 bacteria triples every 5 hours. Which function models the population after t hours? Start 340, multiplier 3, step length 5
f(t)=340·3t5

The wrong choices test the failure points: 3t as a product where the exponent should be, 5/t where t/5 should be, or base 2 (confusing tripling with doubling).

parts.title: Part 7 · Desmos applications
parts.html:
• “After how many years does the population reach 5000?” Type the model and the line y = 5000. The x-coordinate of the intersection is the answer.
  • Comparing growth: type both models. The straight one is linear; the one that curves away is exponential.
  • Radical equations: graph y = √x and y = x − 2. The graph shows only the real intersection, x = 4. The extraneous x = 1 never appears, which makes Desmos a quick check on your algebra.
  • Fraction exponents: Desmos evaluates 82/3 directly. For equivalent-expression questions, plug the same number into the original and each choice and compare the values.

Tip. Logarithms never appear on the Digital SAT. When a question seems to need one (“after how long will the value reach…?”), it is a Desmos intersection question: graph the model and the target value, and read the x-coordinate.

parts.title: Part 8 · Things to remember
parts.html:
• Add or subtract only like terms: same base, same exponent.
  • Same base: multiplying adds the exponents, dividing subtracts them, and a power of a power multiplies them.
  • Same exponent: multiply or divide the bases and keep the exponent.
  • Negative exponent: x−n = 1/xn. Zero exponent: x⁰ = 1 for any x except 0.
  • Roots are fraction exponents: the nth root of xm is xm/n, and roots of the same kind multiply and divide under one root sign.
  • Radical equations: always check the answers in the original equation.
  • Models: in a · bt, a is the starting value and b is the multiplier per step.
